topics.name: Ku Klux Klan
topics.kicker: Hate group founded after the Civil War · Used terror to block Black rights
topics.briefing: The Ku Klux Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865 by six Confederate veterans. During Reconstruction, its masked members used threats and violence to stop Black Americans from voting and to drive out Republican officials, until Congress and President Ulysses S. Grant cracked down with the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. The group came back in 1915 and again during the civil rights movement, and each time Americans fought it in Congress, in the courts, and through peaceful protest.
accept: knights of the ku klux klan

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Part of this group’s name comes from the Greek word for “circle.” It was founded in late 1865 by six Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee, and former Confederate general Nathan Bedford Forrest became its first Grand Wizard.
tossups.r: Congress passed laws against it in 1870 and 1871. For 10 points, name this white supremacist group whose members terrorized Black Americans during Reconstruction.

tossups.p: In 1871, Congress passed a law nicknamed for this group that let President Ulysses S. Grant suspend habeas corpus [“HAY-bee-us KOR-pus”] and use federal troops against it. Grant then suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties, and hundreds of this group’s members were arrested.
tossups.r: Its members hid their faces behind masks. For 10 points, name this secret terrorist group founded in Tennessee after the Civil War.

tossups.p: In 1915, William J. Simmons, a former Methodist preacher who took the title Imperial Wizard, revived this group at a ceremony on Stone Mountain, near Atlanta, Georgia. He was inspired partly by a new film that glorified the group’s Reconstruction-era members.
tossups.r: That film was D. W. Griffith’s _The Birth of a Nation_. For 10 points, name this white supremacist group first founded in 1865.

tossups.p: This group’s power in Indiana collapsed after its state leader, D. C. Stephenson, was convicted of murder in 1925, the same year tens of thousands of its members marched in Washington, D.C. In that decade, it targeted Catholics, Jews, and immigrants as well as Black Americans.
tossups.r: At its peak, it claimed millions of members. For 10 points, name this hooded white supremacist group.

tossups.p: Bobby Frank Cherry, convicted in 2002, was the last of three members of this group found guilty of a 1963 church bombing. That bombing, at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama, killed four Black girls on a Sunday morning.
tossups.r: In the 1960s, its members used violence against the civil rights movement. For 10 points, name this white supremacist group, first founded during Reconstruction.

tossups.p: The FBI code-named its 1964 investigation MIBURN, short for “Mississippi Burning,” after members of this group murdered three civil rights workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, near Philadelphia, Mississippi. In 1967, a federal jury convicted seven men of violating the workers’ civil rights.
tossups.r: The three men had been working to register Black voters during Freedom Summer. For 10 points, name this hooded white supremacist group.

tossups.p: In _Brandenburg v. Ohio_, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of an Ohio leader of this group, ruling that the government may punish speech only when it is meant and likely to cause “imminent lawless action.” That 1969 decision became a major free-speech precedent.
tossups.r: That group had been revived in 1915. For 10 points, name this group whose members wore white hoods and robes.

tossups.p: Attorney General Amos Akerman led the new Department of Justice in prosecuting members of this group, while a congressional committee gathered thousands of pages of testimony about its violence in the South. Those efforts largely broke this group by 1872.
tossups.r: Ulysses S. Grant was president at the time. For 10 points, name this Reconstruction-era group that used terror to keep Black men from voting.

tossups.p: In 1870, North Carolina governor William Holden called out the state militia against this group, in a campaign named the Kirk-Holden War after Holden and his militia commander, George Kirk. The state legislature then impeached Holden, and he became the first U.S. governor removed from office that way.
tossups.r: Its members attacked Black voters and white Republicans across the South. For 10 points, name this group founded by Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee.

tossups.p: Thomas Dixon’s 1905 novel _The Clansman_, which praised this group, became the basis for a 1915 film that President Woodrow Wilson screened at the White House. The NAACP protested that film for its racist picture of Reconstruction.
tossups.r: That film was _The Birth of a Nation_. For 10 points, name this white supremacist group revived in 1915.

tossups.p: In _Virginia v. Black_, the Supreme Court ruled in 2003 that a state may ban cross burning done to intimidate people, but it may not assume that every cross burning is a threat. This group took up cross burning after it was revived in 1915.
tossups.r: Its Reconstruction-era members had hidden their faces behind masks. For 10 points, name this white supremacist organization founded in Pulaski, Tennessee.

tossups.p: With help from the Southern Poverty Law Center, Beulah Mae Donald won a seven-million-dollar lawsuit in 1987 against a large branch of this group after its members murdered her son in Mobile, Alabama. The verdict forced that branch to give up its headquarters building.
tossups.r: Its members had also fought the civil rights movement. For 10 points, name this hate group first founded in 1865 and revived in 1915.

tossups.p: In March 1965, President Lyndon Johnson went on television to announce the arrests of four members of this group for the murder of Viola Liuzzo, a white volunteer from Detroit who had helped with the Selma to Montgomery march.
tossups.r: Johnson urged its members to quit. For 10 points, name this white supremacist organization first founded after the Civil War.

tossups.p: Supreme Court Justice Hugo Black had briefly belonged to this group as an Alabama lawyer in the 1920s, a fact reported by a newspaper soon after he joined the Court in 1937. Black later joined the unanimous ruling in _Brown v. Board of Education_.
tossups.r: In the 1920s, it claimed millions of members. For 10 points, name this white supremacist group that was revived in 1915.

tossups.p: In May 1961, a mob that included members of this group set fire to a Freedom Riders’ bus outside Anniston, Alabama, and members of this group attacked other riders in Birmingham while local police held back.
tossups.r: The Freedom Riders were testing a Supreme Court ruling against segregated bus stations. For 10 points, name this hooded white supremacist group.

trap.title: Group, laws, or era?
trap.body: Questions about Reconstruction and civil rights mention several related answers. The Ku Klux Klan was a secret, violent white supremacist group. Jim Crow laws were the segregation laws Southern states passed later, the Black Codes were laws passed right after the Civil War, and the White League and the Red Shirts were other armed white supremacist groups of the 1870s. Answering “Jim Crow” or “Reconstruction” when the question asks for “this group” is wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This group” or “this organization,” with clues like Pulaski, Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Grand Wizard, Stone Mountain, or _The Birth of a Nation_, means the Ku Klux Klan. “These laws” means Jim Crow laws or the Black Codes, and “this era” means Reconstruction. “KKK” and “the Klan” are both fine.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ku Klux Klan (accept KKK or the Klan)

topics.name: Tobacco
topics.kicker: Cash crop that saved Jamestown · Grown with enslaved labor in the Chesapeake
topics.briefing: Jamestown nearly failed until John Rolfe planted a sweeter kind of tobacco around 1612 and shipped it to England, where it sold for high prices. Soon Virginians were growing it everywhere, even in the streets, and the crop spread across the Chesapeake on the labor of indentured servants and, later, enslaved Africans. The leaf was so valuable that colonists used it as money, paying taxes, fines, and even ministers’ salaries in pounds of tobacco.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This plant’s genus and its best-known chemical are both named for Jean Nicot, a French ambassador who sent it from Portugal to the French royal court around 1560. Native peoples of the Americas had grown it for ceremonies and trade long before Europeans arrived.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe made the cash crop of colonial Virginia.

tossups.p: King James I wrote a 1604 pamphlet called a “Counterblaste” against this substance, describing its use as “loathsome to the eye, hateful to the nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the lungs.” Even so, his own colony in Virginia soon grew rich by selling it.
tossups.r: John Rolfe began growing it there around 1612. For 10 points, name this crop, colonial Virginia’s main export.

tossups.p: In 1617, Deputy Governor Samuel Argall found Jamestown’s colonists growing this crop in the town’s streets and marketplace. A few years later, men in the colony used this crop to pay for the voyages of women who came over as brides.
tossups.r: It had first been planted for export by John Rolfe. For 10 points, name this cash crop, which made Virginia rich.

tossups.p: Patrick Henry first became famous arguing the Parson’s Cause, a 1763 case over a law that let Virginia pay its Anglican ministers in cash instead of in this crop after a drought drove up its price. In colonial Virginia, warehouse receipts for this crop were used as money.
tossups.r: Taxes and fines there were often counted in pounds of it. For 10 points, name this cash crop that John Rolfe made Virginia’s first big export.

tossups.p: Like neighboring Virginia, Lord Baltimore’s colony of Maryland, founded in 1634, came to depend on this crop, and its colonists often paid taxes and debts in pounds of it. Many Chesapeake planters loaded this crop onto ships at their own riverside wharves.
tossups.r: It was the leading export of the Chesapeake colonies. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe first grew for export at Jamestown.

tossups.p: James Buchanan Duke used the Bonsack machine to mass-produce cigarettes and in 1890 formed a giant company that controlled most of the American market for this crop’s products. The Supreme Court broke up that trust in 1911, the same month it broke up Standard Oil.
tossups.r: Duke University is named for his family. For 10 points, name this crop that made Durham, North Carolina, an industrial city.

tossups.p: Colonial planters packed this crop into huge barrels called hogsheads, which were sometimes rolled along “rolling roads” to the docks. A 1730 Virginia law required this crop to be checked at public warehouses before it could be shipped.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cash crop of the Chesapeake colonies, first grown for export by John Rolfe.

tossups.p: Under England’s Navigation Acts, this crop was one of the “enumerated” goods that colonists could ship only to England or other English colonies. In the 1700s, merchants in Glasgow, Scotland, grew rich buying it from Chesapeake planters.
tossups.r: It was first grown for export at Jamestown by John Rolfe. For 10 points, name this crop that made Virginia and Maryland wealthy.

tossups.p: In the 1760s, George Washington stopped growing this crop at Mount Vernon and switched to wheat, partly because it wore out the soil and left him in debt to British merchants. Many Virginia planters moved west as this crop exhausted their land.
tossups.r: It was the main cash crop of colonial Virginia. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe first grew for export at Jamestown.

tossups.p: Architect Benjamin Latrobe designed column tops inside the U.S. Capitol decorated with ears of corn, and others decorated with the leaves and flowers of this plant. Before the Revolution, this crop had been the most valuable export of the thirteen colonies.
tossups.r: It grew mostly in Virginia and Maryland. For 10 points, name this cash crop that John Rolfe made famous in Virginia.

tossups.p: Virginia’s headright system gave fifty acres of land for each person whose passage a planter paid, so planters brought over indentured servants to grow this crop. After Bacon’s Rebellion in 1676, planters relied more and more on enslaved Africans instead.
tossups.r: John Rolfe had begun growing it around 1612. For 10 points, name this crop that dominated the economy of the Chesapeake colonies.

tossups.p: The Powhatan people grew a harsh-tasting kind of this plant that English buyers disliked, so Virginia had little to sell until a sweeter species grown from seeds from Spanish colonies was planted around 1612. That sweeter kind soon sold for high prices in London.
tossups.r: Its grower later married Pocahontas. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe planted to save Jamestown.

tossups.p: Growers of this crop broke off each plant’s flowers in a step called “topping,” so that the plant would grow bigger leaves. After the harvest, workers hung the cut plants in barns to dry, or cure, before packing the leaves into barrels for shipping.
tossups.r: In the 1700s, enslaved people did most of this hard work on Chesapeake plantations. For 10 points, name this cash crop that John Rolfe first grew for export at Jamestown.

tossups.p: In 1839, an enslaved blacksmith named Stephen is credited with discovering a way to cure this crop over charcoal fires that turned its leaves bright yellow. That “bright leaf” variety helped make Durham, North Carolina, a center of the industry built on this crop.
tossups.r: Kentucky became a leading grower of its burley variety. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe first grew for export in Virginia.

tossups.p: In November 1492, two members of Christopher Columbus’s crew exploring Cuba saw Taíno [“tah-EE-noh”] people rolling dried leaves of this plant and smoking them. By 1600, Spanish colonies in the Caribbean and South America were growing it for sale in Europe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plant that John Rolfe made the cash crop of colonial Virginia.

Its genus and the chemical nicotine are named for French diplomat Jean Nicot (around 1560)

trap.title: Which cash crop?
trap.body: Colonial-economy questions often ask for a crop, and four answers get mixed up. Tobacco was the cash crop of Virginia and Maryland, starting with John Rolfe at Jamestown. Rice and indigo were the big crops of colonial South Carolina, where Eliza Lucas Pinckney grew indigo in the 1740s. Cotton took over the Deep South only after Eli Whitney’s cotton gin (1793), and sugar was king in the Caribbean.
trap.fix: Rolfe, Jamestown, the Chesapeake, hogsheads, King James’s “Counterblaste,” the Parson’s Cause, the Dukes of Durham, and “bright leaf” curing mean tobacco. Eliza Lucas means indigo, the cotton gin and “King Cotton” mean cotton, and Caribbean plantations usually mean sugar.

topics.name: William Tecumseh Sherman
topics.kicker: Union general of the Civil War · Led the March to the Sea
topics.briefing: William Tecumseh Sherman, named after the Shawnee leader Tecumseh, was a Union general who captured Atlanta in 1864 and then marched more than 60,000 soldiers across Georgia to Savannah, wrecking railroads, farms, and factories along the way. His March to the Sea brought the war home to Southern civilians and helped end the Civil War. He is remembered for a blunt summary of fighting: “War is hell.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Augustus Saint-Gaudens made a gilded statue of this general on horseback, led by a winged Victory, that stands near Central Park in New York City. When this man died in 1891, his old opponent Joseph E. Johnston stood bareheaded in the rain at his funeral.
tossups.r: Johnston caught pneumonia and died weeks later. For 10 points, name this Union general who led the March to the Sea.

tossups.p: After meeting with Black ministers in Savannah, this general issued Special Field Orders No. 15, which set aside land along the coasts of South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida for freed families in plots of up to 40 acres. Andrew Johnson later returned most of that land to its former owners.
tossups.r: That order inspired the phrase “forty acres and a mule.” For 10 points, name this Union general who had just finished his March to the Sea.

tossups.p: Before the Civil War, this man was the first superintendent of a Louisiana military school that later became Louisiana State University, but he resigned as Louisiana prepared to secede. Earlier, he had been a banker in San Francisco.
tossups.r: He later fought at Shiloh and Vicksburg. For 10 points, name this Union general who captured Atlanta in 1864.

tossups.p: After his father died in 1829, this boy from Lancaster, Ohio, was raised by the family of Thomas Ewing, who later became a senator and the first secretary of the interior. He married Ewing’s daughter Ellen and graduated from West Point in 1840.
tossups.r: His family called him “Cump,” short for a middle name that honored a Shawnee leader. For 10 points, name this Union general who marched from Atlanta to Savannah.

tossups.p: Early in the Civil War, newspapers called this general insane after he told the secretary of war that it would take 200,000 soldiers to win the war in the West, and he was sent home to rest. He recovered and commanded a division at Shiloh.
tossups.r: He later became Ulysses S. Grant’s most trusted general. For 10 points, name this man who led the March to the Sea.

tossups.p: This general’s frontal assault at Kennesaw Mountain failed in June 1864, but he kept moving around Joseph E. Johnston’s army until Jefferson Davis replaced Johnston with John Bell Hood. Hood could not hold the city he was defending.
tossups.r: In September, this general telegraphed, “Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.” For 10 points, name this Union general.

tossups.p: This general wrote to Mayor James Calhoun that “war is cruelty, and you cannot refine it” after ordering civilians to leave the city they lived in. He argued that the people who had brought on the war deserved the hardships it caused them.
tossups.r: He is also remembered for saying that “war is hell.” For 10 points, name this Union general who captured Atlanta.

tossups.p: In December 1864, this general’s soldiers stormed Fort McAllister, opening a supply line to the sea. Days later, he telegraphed Abraham Lincoln to present a city as a “Christmas gift,” along with 150 heavy guns and about 25,000 bales of cotton.
tossups.r: That city was Savannah, the end of his March to the Sea. For 10 points, name this Union general.

tossups.p: At Bennett Place near Durham, North Carolina, this general accepted the surrender of Joseph E. Johnston’s army in April 1865, the largest surrender of the Civil War. Edwin Stanton angrily rejected the generous peace terms this general had first offered Johnston.
tossups.r: Earlier, he had captured Atlanta and Savannah. For 10 points, name this Union general who had led the March to the Sea.

tossups.p: In 1884, this retired general refused the Republican presidential nomination so firmly that a flat refusal to run for office became known by his name. His brother John, a senator from Ohio, sponsored a famous 1890 antitrust law.
tossups.r: Earlier, he had captured Atlanta in 1864. For 10 points, name this Union general famous for his March to the Sea.

tossups.p: After the Civil War, this man served on a peace commission that signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie with the Lakota and other Plains nations. That same year, he signed a treaty that let the Navajo return to their homeland after the Long Walk.
tossups.r: He commanded the U.S. Army from 1869 to 1883. For 10 points, name this Union general who led the March to the Sea.

tossups.p: This general’s soldiers heated railroad rails over bonfires and twisted them around trees, making what were nicknamed his “neckties.” Foragers from his army, called “bummers,” took food and livestock from farms across Georgia, and his army of more than 60,000 men cut a path roughly 60 miles wide.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this general who led the March to the Sea from Atlanta to Savannah.

tossups.p: The M4 tank of World War II was named for this man, and so was a giant sequoia in California that is the largest single tree on Earth by volume. In 1875, he published two volumes of memoirs about his campaigns.
tossups.r: He served under Ulysses S. Grant in the Civil War. For 10 points, name this Union general who captured Atlanta and marched to Savannah.

tossups.p: In February 1865, much of Columbia, South Carolina, burned after this general’s army entered the city, though historians disagree about who started the fires. A month later, his army defeated Joseph E. Johnston at Bentonville, North Carolina.
tossups.r: His army had captured Atlanta the year before. For 10 points, name this Union general whose March to the Sea had ended at Savannah.

tossups.p: This general’s troops were caught by surprise on the first morning of the Battle of Shiloh, and he was wounded in the hand there. In 1864, he replaced Ulysses S. Grant as the top Union commander in the West when Grant went east.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this general who captured Atlanta and led the March to the Sea.

trap.title: Which Sherman? Not Tecumseh!
trap.body: Several famous answers share his name. Roger Sherman of Connecticut proposed the Connecticut Compromise and signed the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution. John Sherman, the general’s younger brother, was the senator behind the Sherman Antitrust Act. And Tecumseh, the Shawnee leader he was named after, is a separate answer line, so saying just “Tecumseh” is wrong.
trap.fix: William Tecumseh Sherman clues: Atlanta, the March to the Sea, Savannah as a “Christmas gift,” Special Field Orders No. 15, and “war is hell.” The Connecticut Compromise means Roger Sherman; antitrust or silver laws mean John Sherman; Prophetstown, Tippecanoe, and the War of 1812 mean Tecumseh. Saying “Sherman” is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: William Tecumseh Sherman (do not accept “Tecumseh”)

topics.name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
topics.kicker: Japan’s surprise attack on Hawaii · Brought the U.S. into World War II
topics.briefing: Early on Sunday morning, December 7, 1941, more than 350 Japanese planes from six aircraft carriers struck the U.S. Navy base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours they sank or damaged eight battleships, and more than 2,400 Americans were killed, including 1,177 crew members of the USS _Arizona_. The next day, President Franklin Roosevelt called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy,” and the United States entered World War II.
topics.answerHtml: attack on Pearl Harbor (accept Hawaii Operation or Operation Z; prompt on Hawaii, Oahu, or Honolulu)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On the morning of this attack, Army privates Joseph Lockard and George Elliott spotted a huge group of incoming planes on radar at Opana Point, but a lieutenant told them not to worry, since he thought the planes were American B-17 bombers expected from California.
tossups.r: The first attackers arrived less than an hour later. For 10 points, name this surprise attack on a U.S. naval base in Hawaii on December 7, 1941.

tossups.p: Before the air raid began, the destroyer USS _Ward_ fired the first American shots of this battle and sank a Japanese midget submarine. Another midget submarine ran aground, and its commander, Kazuo Sakamaki, became the first Japanese prisoner of war captured by the United States.
tossups.r: Franklin Roosevelt said the date of this attack would “live in infamy.” For 10 points, name this December 7, 1941, Japanese attack on a Hawaiian naval base.

tossups.p: Commander Mitsuo Fuchida [“foo-CHEE-dah”] radioed the code words “Tora! Tora! Tora!” to report that this attack had caught its target completely by surprise. Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo [“CHOO-ee-chee nah-GOO-moh”] commanded the six aircraft carriers that launched it, and he decided not to send a third wave that might have destroyed the base’s fuel tanks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this attack on December 7, 1941, that brought the United States into World War II.

tossups.p: This attack’s strike force sailed from the Kuril Islands in late November and kept radio silence as it crossed the North Pacific. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto [“ee-soh-ROH-koo yah-mah-MOH-toh”] planned it, hoping to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet so Japan could seize oil and other resources in Southeast Asia.
tossups.r: It came on December 7, 1941. For 10 points, name this surprise attack on a U.S. naval base in Hawaii.

tossups.p: Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana cast the only vote in Congress against declaring war on Japan the day after this attack. Rankin had also voted against entering World War I in 1917. Days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 7, 1941, attack whose date Franklin Roosevelt said would “live in infamy.”

tossups.p: Doris “Dorie” Miller, a cook aboard the battleship USS _West Virginia_, carried wounded sailors to safety and fired an anti-aircraft machine gun he had never been trained to use during this attack. He became the first African American to receive the Navy Cross.
tossups.r: In 2020, the Navy announced it would name an aircraft carrier for Miller. For 10 points, name this Japanese attack on a Hawaiian naval base on December 7, 1941.

tossups.p: After this attack, Admiral Husband Kimmel and General Walter Short, the Navy and Army commanders in Hawaii, were removed from their commands, and the Roberts Commission blamed them for failing to prepare. Congress held its own long investigation of this attack in 1945 and 1946.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this surprise attack that brought the United States into World War II.

tossups.p: Japanese diplomats Kichisaburo Nomura and Saburo Kurusu handed Secretary of State Cordell Hull a long message breaking off talks after this attack had already begun. American codebreakers in a program called MAGIC had decoded that message before it was delivered.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 7, 1941, attack on a U.S. naval base in Hawaii.

tossups.p: Elvis Presley gave a 1961 benefit concert that helped pay for a white memorial, designed by Alfred Preis, that stretches across the sunken hull of a battleship destroyed in this attack. That memorial was dedicated in 1962.
tossups.r: The battleship, the USS _Arizona_, lost 1,177 crew members. For 10 points, name this December 7, 1941, attack.

tossups.p: This attack missed the Pacific Fleet’s aircraft carriers, which were away from port that morning, and it left the base’s fuel tanks and repair shops largely undamaged. Six months later, at Midway, the U.S. Navy sank four of the six Japanese carriers that had carried out this attack.
tossups.r: It also sank or damaged eight U.S. battleships. For 10 points, name this Japanese surprise attack on December 7, 1941.

tossups.p: The USS _Nevada_ was the only battleship to get underway during this attack before it was run aground on purpose, and the USS _Oklahoma_ capsized. Those ships were moored along Ford Island in an area called Battleship Row.
tossups.r: It came on December 7, 1941. For 10 points, name this attack in which the USS _Arizona_ was destroyed.

tossups.p: The coded message “Climb Mount Niitaka” told the Japanese strike force to go ahead with this attack. Commander Minoru Genda helped plan it, and its torpedoes were fitted with wooden fins so they could run in the shallow water of the harbor.
tossups.r: More than 2,400 Americans were killed in it. For 10 points, name this December 7, 1941, attack on a Hawaiian naval base.

tossups.p: Fear and prejudice after this attack led Franklin Roosevelt to sign Executive Order 9066, which forced about 120,000 Japanese Americans on the West Coast into incarceration camps. The Doolittle Raid on Tokyo in April 1942 was partly meant to strike back after this attack.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this attack on December 7, 1941, “a date which will live in infamy.”

tossups.p: In 1887, the Kingdom of Hawaii renewed a trade treaty that gave the United States the exclusive right to use this place as a naval coaling and repair station. In 1940, Franklin Roosevelt kept the Pacific Fleet based here instead of in California, hoping to discourage Japanese expansion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this harbor on Oahu, the target of a Japanese surprise attack on December 7, 1941.

tossups.p: During this attack, Japanese planes also struck Hickam and Wheeler airfields, destroying many U.S. planes that had been parked close together to guard against sabotage. Within hours, Japan also attacked the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, and Hong Kong.
tossups.r: The next day, Congress declared war on Japan. For 10 points, name this attack on a Hawaiian naval base on December 7, 1941.

Franklin Roosevelt called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy” and asked Congress to declare war
Brought the United States into World War II
The battleship USS _Arizona_ exploded and sank; 1,177 of its crew died, and a memorial spans the wreck
The base is on the island of Oahu, near Honolulu; Hawaii was then a U.S. territory, not a state
Planned by Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet
More than 350 planes from six Japanese aircraft carriers struck in two waves
Eight U.S. battleships were sunk or damaged along Battleship Row, next to Ford Island
More than 2,400 Americans were killed
U.S. aircraft carriers were away from port, and the base’s fuel tanks and repair shops were left largely undamaged
Japan attacked after the U.S. cut off oil sales in 1941 to stop its expansion; it wanted Southeast Asia’s resources
Congress declared war on Japan on December 8 with one “no” vote, Jeannette Rankin’s; Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. on December 11
Cook Doris “Dorie” Miller became the first African American awarded the Navy Cross
Afterward, Executive Order 9066 forced about 120,000 Japanese Americans into incarceration camps
Commander Mitsuo Fuchida radioed “Tora! Tora! Tora!” to signal complete surprise
Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo led the carrier force and skipped a third wave; Minoru Genda helped plan the attack
Radar operators at Opana Point spotted the planes but were told not to worry (they were thought to be B-17s)
The destroyer USS _Ward_ fired the first U.S. shots, sinking a midget submarine
Kazuo Sakamaki became the first Japanese prisoner of war captured by the U.S.
Admiral Husband Kimmel and General Walter Short lost their commands; the Roberts Commission blamed them
Diplomats Nomura and Kurusu gave Cordell Hull Japan’s message breaking off talks after the attack began; MAGIC codebreakers had already decoded it
Coded order “Climb Mount Niitaka”; the strike force sailed from the Kuril Islands under radio silence
Its torpedoes had wooden fins so they could run in the shallow harbor
At Midway (June 1942), the U.S. sank four of the six carriers that had attacked
Alfred Preis designed the USS _Arizona_ Memorial (1962); Elvis Presley gave a benefit concert for it (1961)
The USS _Oklahoma_ capsized; the USS _Nevada_ was the only battleship to get underway
An 1887 treaty with the Kingdom of Hawaii gave the U.S. the right to use the harbor; FDR kept the Pacific Fleet there from 1940
Hickam and Wheeler airfields were hit; planes parked close together to guard against sabotage were destroyed

trap.title: Attack, harbor, or ship?
trap.body: Most tossups ask for the attack, and saying “Pearl Harbor” is enough. But some questions want a related answer: the USS _Arizona_ (“this battleship”), Hawaii or Oahu (“this island” or “this territory”), the Battle of Midway (the June 1942 battle where the U.S. sank four of the attacking carriers), or the Doolittle Raid (the April 1942 bombing of Tokyo). Answering “USS Arizona” when the question wants the attack is wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this attack,” “this event,” “this harbor,” or “this naval base” means Pearl Harbor; “this ship” or “this battleship” means the USS _Arizona_ (or another ship); “this battle” in June 1942 means Midway. If you say only “Hawaii,” expect a prompt, so be ready to add “Pearl Harbor.”
trap.line: Real answer line: attack on Pearl Harbor (accept Hawaii Operation or Operation Z; prompt on Hawaii, Oahu, or Honolulu)

topics.name: Cherokee
topics.kicker: Native nation of the Southeast · Sequoyah’s syllabary and forced removal
topics.briefing: Around 1821, a Cherokee silversmith named Sequoyah did something almost no one in history has done alone: he invented a complete writing system for his people’s language. Within a few years, thousands of Cherokee could read, and they printed their own newspaper, the _Cherokee Phoenix_. Even after the Supreme Court ruled in its favor, the Cherokee Nation was forced off its Southeastern homeland in 1838, and it rebuilt its government in present-day Oklahoma.
topics.answerHtml: Cherokee (accept Cherokee Nation or Tsalagi; prompt on Five Civilized Tribes; do not accept “Trail of Tears”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This people’s language is the only member of the southern branch of the Iroquoian [“eer-uh-KWOY-un”] language family. Around 1821, a silversmith who could not read English finished a system of symbols for the syllables of that language, and within a few years thousands of this people had learned to read with it.
tossups.r: Its inventor was Sequoyah [“sih-KWOY-uh”]. For 10 points, name this Native American nation forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Former U.S. Attorney General William Wirt argued this nation’s 1831 lawsuit against Georgia before the Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Court could not hear the case, because this nation was not a foreign country but one of the “domestic dependent nations.”
tossups.r: Its Principal Chief was John Ross. For 10 points, name this Native American nation removed from Georgia on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Major Ridge, his son John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot [“BOO-dih-noh”] led a small Treaty Party that agreed to give up this nation’s homeland without the approval of most of its people. All three men were killed in 1839 by members of this nation who were angry about that treaty.
tossups.r: The treaty was signed at New Echota [“eh-CHOH-tuh”] in 1835. For 10 points, name this nation forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Elias Boudinot [“BOO-dih-noh”] edited this people’s newspaper, the _Phoenix_, which began printing in 1828 at their capital of New Echota [“eh-CHOH-tuh”]. Printed in English and in this people’s own language, it was the first newspaper published by Native Americans.
tossups.r: Its type used the syllabary invented by Sequoyah [“sih-KWOY-uh”]. For 10 points, name this nation that was forced west on the Trail of Tears in 1838.

tossups.p: In 1827, this nation adopted a written constitution that created three branches of government, much like the U.S. Constitution. The next year, its legislature chose a Principal Chief who held that post for nearly forty years, leading his people through removal and the Civil War.
tossups.r: That chief was John Ross. For 10 points, name this nation whose homeland in Georgia was taken after the Indian Removal Act.

tossups.p: After gold was discovered near Dahlonega [“duh-LON-uh-guh”] in 1829, Georgia passed laws claiming this nation’s land and began giving it away to white settlers in lotteries. Because Georgia also banned this nation’s government from meeting in the state, its council moved to Red Clay, Tennessee.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation led by John Ross, which was forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: In 1838, soldiers under General Winfield Scott forced thousands of this people out of their homes and into crowded stockades. The next year, survivors rebuilt their government in the West and made Tahlequah [“TAL-uh-kwah”] their new capital.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Native American nation whose forced removal from the Southeast is called the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Members of this nation who stayed in the mountains of North Carolina avoided removal, and their descendants make up the Eastern Band, whose land is called the Qualla [“KWAH-luh”] Boundary. Another federally recognized tribe of this people is the United Keetoowah [“kee-TOO-wah”] Band.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this people, whose writing system was created by Sequoyah and most of whom were forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Stand Watie, a member of this nation, became a Confederate general and was the last Confederate general in the field to surrender, in June 1865. His brother, Elias Boudinot [“BOO-dih-noh”], had signed the treaty that gave away this nation’s eastern homeland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, led for decades by John Ross, whose removal was called the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Dragging Canoe opposed a 1775 deal at Sycamore Shoals that sold much of present-day Kentucky to Richard Henderson’s Transylvania Company. He then led a band of this people called the Chickamauga [“chik-uh-MAW-guh”] in years of war against American settlers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, whose writing system was later created by Sequoyah, that was forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: At the 1814 Battle of Horseshoe Bend, hundreds of warriors from this nation fought on Andrew Jackson’s side against the Red Stick Creeks. By the 1830s, this nation’s homeland covered parts of Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama.
tossups.r: Jackson later signed the Indian Removal Act. For 10 points, name this nation forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Wilma Mankiller became the first woman to serve as this nation’s Principal Chief, leading it from 1985 to 1995, and she later appeared on a U.S. quarter. The humorist Will Rogers had been born a citizen of this nation in Indian Territory.
tossups.r: This nation’s capital is Tahlequah, Oklahoma. For 10 points, name this nation, which was forced west on the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Nancy Ward held the title “Beloved Woman” among this people, who were organized into seven clans and traced family membership through their mothers. During the American Revolution, Ward urged peace and warned American settlers about planned attacks.
tossups.r: Sequoyah [“sih-KWOY-uh”] later created a writing system for this people. For 10 points, name this nation, one of the “Five Civilized Tribes,” that the U.S. forced west in 1838.

tossups.p: John Ross sent Congress petitions signed by thousands of his people, protesting a treaty that traded this nation’s eastern lands for five million dollars and land in the West. The U.S. Senate approved that treaty anyway in 1836.
tossups.r: That treaty was signed by a small Treaty Party at New Echota. For 10 points, name this nation whose removal became known as the Trail of Tears.

tossups.p: Missionaries Samuel Worcester and Elizur Butler were sentenced to hard labor for living among this people without a license from Georgia. When the Supreme Court overturned their convictions, Andrew Jackson supposedly said, “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it.”
tossups.r: That 1832 case was _Worcester v. Georgia_. For 10 points, name this nation forced west on the Trail of Tears.

clues.t: Forced west to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) on the Trail of Tears, 1838–1839
Sequoyah, a silversmith, created their writing system, a syllabary, around 1821
A Native nation of the Southeast (Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, Alabama); one of the “Five Civilized Tribes”
Lost their homeland after the Indian Removal Act, signed by President Andrew Jackson in 1830
John Ross, Principal Chief from 1828 to 1866, fought removal with lawsuits and petitions
_Worcester v. Georgia_ (1832): John Marshall’s Supreme Court said Georgia’s laws had no force on their land, but Georgia and Jackson ignored the ruling
Treaty of New Echota (1835): a small Treaty Party traded their eastern land for $5 million and land in the West
Their newspaper, the _Phoenix_ (1828), edited by Elias Boudinot, was the first newspaper published by Native Americans
In their 1831 case against Georgia (argued by William Wirt), John Marshall called Native nations “domestic dependent nations”
In 1838, General Winfield Scott’s soldiers forced them into stockades before the march west
An 1829 gold rush near Dahlonega made Georgia push harder to take their land, which it gave away in lotteries
Adopted a written constitution with three branches in 1827, modeled on the U.S. Constitution
Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot led the Treaty Party; all three were killed in 1839
Capitals: New Echota, Georgia (from 1825); Red Clay, Tennessee (1832–1838); Tahlequah, Oklahoma (from 1839)
The syllabary has 85 characters, each standing for a syllable; their language is Iroquoian
Some stayed in North Carolina; their descendants form the Eastern Band (Qualla Boundary). The United Keetoowah Band is in Oklahoma
Stand Watie, Elias Boudinot’s brother, was the last Confederate general in the field to surrender (June 1865)
Dragging Canoe opposed the 1775 Sycamore Shoals land sale and led the Chickamauga in war against settlers
Their warriors fought on Andrew Jackson’s side against the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend (1814)
Wilma Mankiller was the first woman Principal Chief (1985–1995) and appears on a 2022 U.S. quarter
The humorist Will Rogers was born a citizen of their nation in Indian Territory (1879)
Nancy Ward, honored as a “Beloved Woman,” urged peace during the American Revolution
Organized into seven clans; family membership passed through the mother
Missionaries Samuel Worcester and Elizur Butler were sentenced to hard labor for living among them without a Georgia license

trap.title: People or event?
trap.body: Most Cherokee clues, like John Ross, the Treaty of New Echota, Winfield Scott, and _Worcester v. Georgia_, also lead tossups on the Trail of Tears, Indian removal, and Andrew Jackson. If the question asks for “this nation” or “this people,” answering “Trail of Tears” is wrong. It is also easy to name the wrong member of the “Five Civilized Tribes,” since all five were forced west in the 1830s.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this nation” or “this people” wants Cherokee, while “this event” or “this march” wants the Trail of Tears. Sequoyah, the _Phoenix_ newspaper, and Tahlequah mean Cherokee; Osceola means Seminole, the Red Sticks were Creek, and Dancing Rabbit Creek means Choctaw.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cherokee (accept Cherokee Nation or Tsalagi; prompt on Five Civilized Tribes; do not accept “Trail of Tears”)

topics.name: Connecticut
topics.kicker: New England colony and state · The Fundamental Orders and the Charter Oak
topics.briefing: This small New England state calls itself the “Constitution State” because in 1639 its first towns adopted the Fundamental Orders, often called the first written constitution in the Western world. According to legend, its colonists hid their royal charter in an oak tree to keep it from a royal governor. The state also gave America Nathan Hale, Noah Webster’s dictionary, and the nation’s oldest continuously published newspaper, the _Hartford Courant_.
topics.answerHtml: Connecticut (accept Connecticut Colony or Colony of Connecticut; prompt on “Constitution State” or “Nutmeg State”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1638 sermon, a Puritan minister argued that “the foundation of authority is laid” in “the free consent of the people.” Two years earlier, that minister had led his congregation from Massachusetts Bay to found a new town on a river in this colony.
tossups.r: That minister, Thomas Hooker, inspired the Fundamental Orders of 1639. For 10 points, name this colony, later the “Constitution State.”

tossups.p: According to legend, the candles at a 1687 meeting were suddenly blown out, and this colony’s royal charter disappeared before Sir Edmund Andros could take it away. The charter was said to be hidden in a hollow oak tree, which appears on this state’s 1999 quarter.
tossups.r: That tree was the Charter Oak. For 10 points, name this New England state whose capital is Hartford.

tossups.p: In 1637, English soldiers led by John Mason attacked and burned a fortified Pequot [“PEE-kwot”] village near the Mystic River, killing hundreds of people. A treaty signed the next year ended that war and opened the Pequot homeland in this colony to English settlers.
tossups.r: That conflict was the Pequot War. For 10 points, name this colony where Thomas Hooker founded Hartford.

tossups.p: Roger Sherman of this state is the only person who signed the Continental Association, the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution. With Oliver Ellsworth, Sherman proposed a plan for a two-house Congress that is named after this state.
tossups.r: That plan is also called the Great Compromise. For 10 points, name this state, the fifth to ratify the Constitution.

tossups.p: This state’s official hero was a young schoolteacher who volunteered to spy on the British in New York in 1776. After he was captured and executed, he was remembered for supposedly saying, “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.”
tossups.r: That hero was Nathan Hale. For 10 points, name this state, home to Yale University in New Haven.

tossups.p: In 1781, a traitor born in this state’s town of Norwich led British troops in a raid that burned much of New London. During that raid, the British also captured Fort Griswold, across the Thames [“THAYMZ”] River in Groton.
tossups.r: That traitor was Benedict Arnold. For 10 points, name this state on Long Island Sound, whose capital is Hartford.

tossups.p: In 1839, Africans who had been illegally enslaved took over the Spanish schooner _La Amistad_ and were captured off Long Island and jailed in this state. Their leader, Sengbe Pieh, also called Cinqué [“sin-KAY”], and the others were freed after John Quincy Adams argued their case before the Supreme Court.
tossups.r: That ship’s name is Spanish for “friendship.” For 10 points, name this state, home to Yale University in New Haven.

tossups.p: Prudence Crandall, this state’s official heroine, opened a school for African American girls in the town of Canterbury in 1833. Lawmakers responded by passing a “Black Law” to shut it down, and Crandall was arrested and put on trial.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England state, whose capital, Hartford, stands on a river that shares its name.

tossups.p: Moses Cleaveland led a surveying party for a land company from this state and founded a settlement on Lake Erie in 1796 that grew into a city named for him. That city lies in northeastern Ohio, on land this state had kept as its “Western Reserve.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England state, whose river towns adopted the Fundamental Orders in 1639.

tossups.p: Mark Twain lived in this state’s capital during the years he wrote _Adventures of Huckleberry Finn_, and the hero of another of his novels is a factory superintendent from that city who wakes up in King Arthur’s court.
tossups.r: Twain’s neighbor there was Harriet Beecher Stowe. For 10 points, name this New England state, whose capital is Hartford.

tossups.p: In 1814, New England Federalists who opposed the War of 1812 met in secret in this state’s capital, where some delegates talked about leaving the Union. Their demands reached Washington just as news arrived of the Treaty of Ghent and Andrew Jackson’s victory at New Orleans.
tossups.r: That meeting was the Hartford Convention. For 10 points, name this New England state that hosted it, the fifth to ratify the Constitution.

tossups.p: This state’s name comes from an Algonquian word meaning “long tidal river.” The Dutch explorer Adriaen Block [“AH-dree-ahn”] sailed up that river in 1614, and in 1633 the Dutch built a trading post called the House of Hope on the site of this state’s future capital.
tossups.r: That river is the longest in New England. For 10 points, name this state, which shares its name with that river.

tossups.p: This state’s highest point is on the slope of Mount Frissell [“FRIZ-ul”], whose summit lies across the border in Massachusetts. Only Rhode Island and Delaware are smaller than this state, where the first nuclear-powered submarine, the USS _Nautilus_, was built in Groton.
tossups.r: The U.S. Coast Guard Academy is in its city of New London. For 10 points, name this state on Long Island Sound, whose capital is Hartford.

tossups.p: During the Great Awakening, Jonathan Edwards preached “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” in 1741 at Enfield, a town that is now part of this state. Later, Noah Webster, a native of this state, published his _American Dictionary of the English Language_ in 1828.
tossups.r: This colony’s college, founded in 1701, became Yale University. For 10 points, name this New England state.

tossups.p: Jonathan Trumbull, this colony’s governor when the Revolution began, was the only colonial governor then in office to side with the Patriots. His colony sent so much food and other supplies to the Continental Army that it was nicknamed the “Provisions State.”
tossups.r: Trumbull’s son John painted _Declaration of Independence_. For 10 points, name this state, whose capital is Hartford.

clues.t: Nicknamed the “Constitution State” for the Fundamental Orders; also called the “Nutmeg State”
Capital: Hartford; its city of New Haven is home to Yale University (founded 1701)
One of the 13 colonies; became the 5th state to ratify the Constitution (January 1788)
New England state on Long Island Sound, between New York and Rhode Island, with Massachusetts to the north
Shares its name with its great river, the longest river in New England
Puritan minister Thomas Hooker led his congregation from Massachusetts Bay to found Hartford (1636)
Fundamental Orders (1639): Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield set up a government, often called the first written constitution
Charter Oak: legend says colonists hid their 1662 royal charter in an oak to keep it from Sir Edmund Andros (1687)
Nathan Hale, the official state hero, was executed as a spy in 1776 (“I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country”)
Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Great Compromise (1787), which is also named for this state
Benedict Arnold was born in Norwich; in 1781 he led the British raid that burned New London
Pequot War (1636–1638): English soldiers attacked a Pequot fort near the Mystic River in 1637, killing hundreds
Mark Twain lived in Hartford next door to Harriet Beecher Stowe, who was born in Litchfield
Hooker’s 1638 sermon: “the foundation of authority is laid” in “the free consent of the people”
Name from an Algonquian word for “long tidal river”; Adriaen Block explored the river (1614); the Dutch built the House of Hope at Hartford (1633)
Roger Sherman was the only person to sign the Continental Association, the Declaration, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution
Governor Jonathan Trumbull was the only colonial governor in office when the war began to side with the Patriots; the colony was called the “Provisions State”
_Amistad_ (1839): Africans led by Sengbe Pieh (Cinqué) were jailed there before the Supreme Court freed them (1841)
Prudence Crandall, the state heroine, opened a school for African American girls in Canterbury (1833)
Its “Western Reserve” in Ohio: Moses Cleaveland of its land company founded Cleveland (1796)
Hartford Convention (1814–1815): New England Federalists met in secret to protest the War of 1812
Third-smallest state; highest point on Mount Frissell’s slope; the USS _Nautilus_ was built at Groton; the Coast Guard Academy is in New London
Jonathan Edwards preached “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” at Enfield (1741); native Noah Webster published his dictionary (1828)
The _Hartford Courant_ (1764) is the nation’s oldest continuously published newspaper

trap.title: Which runaway Puritan?
trap.body: Three famous Puritans left Massachusetts Bay in the 1630s, and each started somewhere different. Thomas Hooker led his congregation to Hartford, in Connecticut, while Roger Williams founded Providence and Anne Hutchinson settled nearby, both in what became Rhode Island. Players who hear “left Massachusetts” often buzz with Rhode Island too early, and “first written constitution” clues can tempt you toward the Mayflower Compact.
trap.fix: Hooker, Hartford, the Fundamental Orders, the Charter Oak, and the Pequot War mean Connecticut. Williams, Providence, religious freedom, and Hutchinson mean Rhode Island. The Mayflower Compact (1620) belongs to Plymouth, which later joined Massachusetts.
trap.line: Real answer line: Connecticut (accept Connecticut Colony or Colony of Connecticut; prompt on “Constitution State” or “Nutmeg State”)

topics.name: Cornelius Vanderbilt
topics.kicker: Steamboat and railroad tycoon · The “Commodore” of the Gilded Age
topics.briefing: At 16, Cornelius Vanderbilt borrowed $100 from his mother to buy a small sailboat and ferry passengers between Staten Island and Manhattan. He went on to run fleets of steamboats, earning the nickname “the Commodore,” and then took over railroads like the New York Central. When he died in 1877, he was the richest man in America, and his $1 million gift had created Vanderbilt University.
topics.answerHtml: Cornelius Vanderbilt (accept “Commodore Vanderbilt”; prompt on “the Commodore”; do not accept “William Henry Vanderbilt”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young man, this captain ran Thomas Gibbons’s steamboat _Bellona_ between New Jersey and New York City, defying a monopoly that New York had granted to Robert Fulton and Robert Livingston. The Supreme Court struck down that monopoly in _Gibbons v. Ogden_ in 1824.
tossups.r: This man later built a railroad empire. For 10 points, name this tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore,” who controlled the New York Central Railroad.

tossups.p: At age 16, this man borrowed 100 dollars from his mother to buy a periauger, a small sailing barge, and began ferrying passengers and freight between Staten Island and Manhattan. His later fleets of steamboats earned him a naval-sounding nickname.
tossups.r: That nickname was “the Commodore.” For 10 points, name this tycoon who later took over the New York Central Railroad.

tossups.p: During the California Gold Rush, this man’s Accessory Transit Company carried travelers by steamship up the San Juan River and across Lake Nicaragua, a shorter route to California than crossing Panama.
tossups.r: He later helped topple William Walker, who seized that company’s property. For 10 points, name this steamboat and railroad tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: In the 1868 Erie War, this man tried to buy control of a railroad, but Daniel Drew, Jay Gould, and James Fisk kept issuing new shares of stock. Those rivals then fled across the Hudson River to Jersey City with millions of dollars from the stock they had sold him.
tossups.r: This man had already taken over the New York Central. For 10 points, name this Gilded Age tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: In 1870, this tycoon helped Victoria Woodhull and her sister Tennessee Claflin open the first Wall Street brokerage firm run by women. Two years later, Woodhull became the first woman to run for president of the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this steamboat and railroad magnate, whose one-million-dollar gift founded a university in Nashville.

tossups.p: This man bought control of the New York and Harlem Railroad and the Hudson River Railroad in the 1860s. In 1871, he opened Grand Central Depot in Manhattan, and a bronze statue of him stands outside the terminal that later replaced it.
tossups.r: He also took over the New York Central. For 10 points, name this railroad tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: In 1853, this man took his family on a grand tour of Europe aboard his new steam yacht, the _North Star_. While he was away, two former associates took control of the company he had founded to carry Gold Rush travelers across Nicaragua.
tossups.r: He later controlled the New York Central Railroad. For 10 points, name this tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: This man’s grandsons built some of the grandest homes of the Gilded Age, including The Breakers in Newport, Rhode Island, and the Biltmore Estate in North Carolina. Most of this man’s fortune went to his son William Henry, who roughly doubled it.
tossups.r: Bishop Holland McTyeire persuaded this man to fund a university in Nashville. For 10 points, name this tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: During the Civil War, this man gave the Union Navy a huge steamship named after himself, hoping it could ram the Confederate ironclad _Virginia_. Earlier, his steamships had competed for passengers across the Atlantic Ocean.
tossups.r: He later built Grand Central Depot. For 10 points, name this tycoon who controlled the New York Central Railroad.

tossups.p: This man became famous for steamboat fare wars, cutting ticket prices so low that some rival companies paid him to stop running boats on their routes. He was born in 1794 on Staten Island.
tossups.r: His fleets earned him the nickname “the Commodore.” For 10 points, name this man who later built a railroad empire around the New York Central.

tossups.p: When this man died in 1877, his fortune of about 100 million dollars was the largest in the United States. Critics called him a “robber baron,” a label also given to men like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore,” whose name is on a university in Nashville.

tossups.p: The filibuster William Walker, who seized power in Nicaragua in 1855, gave this man’s transit company to rival businessmen. This man struck back by helping the Central American armies that forced Walker to surrender in 1857.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore,” who later ran the New York Central Railroad.

tossups.p: This man’s great-great-granddaughter Gloria became a famous artist and fashion designer, and her son, Anderson Cooper, became a CNN news anchor. This man himself started out ferrying passengers across New York Harbor from Staten Island.
tossups.r: He later took over the New York Central Railroad. For 10 points, name this tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: After switching from ships to railroads in the 1860s, this man took over the Hudson River Railroad and, in 1867, a larger line running west from Albany to Buffalo. In 1869, he merged the two into one company.
tossups.r: That larger line was the New York Central. For 10 points, name this Gilded Age tycoon nicknamed “the Commodore.”

tossups.p: T. J. Stiles won a Pulitzer Prize for _The First Tycoon_, a biography of this man. It describes how he rose from running a single ferryboat out of Staten Island to building a shipping and railroad empire worth about 100 million dollars.
tossups.r: His one-million-dollar gift founded a university in Nashville. For 10 points, name this business titan nicknamed “the Commodore.”

Railroad tycoon who controlled the New York Central Railroad
His $1 million gift (1873) founded a university in Nashville, Tennessee, that bears his name
Gilded Age “robber baron”; the richest American when he died in 1877 (about $100 million)
Born on Staten Island (1794); at 16 he borrowed $100 from his mother to buy a periauger and ferry passengers to Manhattan
Captained steamboats for Thomas Gibbons, defying the Fulton–Livingston monopoly that _Gibbons v. Ogden_ (1824) struck down
