Opened Grand Central Depot in Manhattan (1871); his statue stands outside Grand Central Terminal
During the Gold Rush, his Accessory Transit Company carried travelers to California across Nicaragua
Helped bring down William Walker, the filibuster who seized power in Nicaragua and gave away his transit company
Won steamboat fare wars by cutting prices; some rivals paid him to leave their routes
Ran Thomas Gibbons’s steamboat _Bellona_ between New Jersey and New York City
Took over the New York and Harlem and Hudson River railroads, won the New York Central (1867), and merged lines (1869)
Toured Europe with his family on his steam yacht _North Star_ (1853)
Gave the Union Navy a huge steamship named for himself to fight the ironclad _Virginia_ (1862)
Backed Victoria Woodhull and Tennessee Claflin, the first women to run a Wall Street brokerage (1870)
Methodist bishop Holland McTyeire persuaded him to fund the university in Nashville
In the Erie War, his rivals fled to Jersey City with millions from the stock they had sold him
Left most of his fortune to his son William Henry, who roughly doubled it
Grandsons built The Breakers (Newport) and the Biltmore Estate (North Carolina); great-great-granddaughter Gloria was Anderson Cooper’s mother
Subject of T. J. Stiles’s Pulitzer Prize–winning biography _The First Tycoon_

trap.title: Which steamboat man?
trap.body: Early clues about steamboats, railroads, and huge fortunes fit several men. Robert Fulton built the famous early steamboat and held the New York monopoly, and Thomas Gibbons won _Gibbons v. Ogden_, but Vanderbilt was the young captain who worked for Gibbons. In the Erie War, his rivals were Jay Gould, James Fisk, and Daniel Drew. His son William Henry Vanderbilt, who inherited most of the fortune, is a different person, so “William Vanderbilt” is wrong.
trap.fix: Ferries from Staten Island, the _Bellona_, “the Commodore,” the Nicaragua route, Grand Central Depot, the New York Central, and a university in Nashville all mean Cornelius Vanderbilt. Saying just “Vanderbilt” is fine, but never “William.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Cornelius Vanderbilt (accept “Commodore Vanderbilt”; prompt on “the Commodore”; do not accept “William Henry Vanderbilt”)

topics.name: Cotton
topics.kicker: Fiber crop that ruled the antebellum South · Whitney’s gin and “King Cotton”
topics.briefing: In 1793, Eli Whitney built a simple machine, the cotton gin, that pulled the sticky seeds out of cotton fibers far faster than hands could. Growing cotton suddenly paid huge profits, and planters forced enslaved people to clear and work new fields from Georgia to Texas; by 1860, nearly 4 million people were enslaved in the United States. Southerners boasted that “Cotton is King,” and the crop fed textile mills from Massachusetts to England.
topics.answerHtml: Cotton (accept Gossypium; prompt on “cash crop”; do not accept “cotton gin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At Mulberry Grove, a Georgia plantation owned by Catharine Greene, a young Yale graduate built a machine whose wire teeth pulled the fibers of this plant through slots too narrow for its seeds. Planters across the South soon copied that 1793 invention, so its inventor earned little from it.
tossups.r: That machine was Eli Whitney’s gin. For 10 points, name this fiber crop that became the South’s most valuable export.

tossups.p: In an 1858 speech, Senator James Henry Hammond of South Carolina warned Northerners, “You dare not make war” on this crop, claiming that no power on earth would dare to. His speech helped popularize a famous slogan of the antebellum South.
tossups.r: That slogan declared this crop “King.” For 10 points, name this crop whose seeds were removed by Eli Whitney’s gin.

tossups.p: During the American Civil War, textile mills in Lancashire, England, ran so short of this raw material that hundreds of thousands of workers lost their jobs or had their hours cut. In 1863, Abraham Lincoln wrote to the workingmen of Manchester to thank them for supporting the Union despite their hardship.
tossups.r: Britain found new supplies in Egypt and India. For 10 points, name this crop that the Confederacy hoped would force Britain to support it.

tossups.p: In 1919, the town of Enterprise, Alabama, put up a monument to a pest that had destroyed so much of this crop that local farmers switched to growing peanuts. That beetle had crossed from Mexico into Texas in the 1890s.
tossups.r: That pest was the boll weevil. For 10 points, name this crop that enslaved people were forced to plant and pick across the Deep South.

tossups.p: Samuel Slater memorized the designs of British spinning machines and built a water-powered mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, to spin this fiber into thread. Decades later, the Boston Associates built huge mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, where young “mill girls” wove it into cloth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fiber, picked by enslaved workers in the South and spun in Northern textile mills.

tossups.p: In the 1840s, Massachusetts Whigs split between “Conscience Whigs,” who opposed slavery, and a faction close to factory owners, nicknamed for the raw material their mills bought from Southern plantations. Conscience Whigs said that faction put business ties with the South ahead of opposing slavery.
tossups.r: Charles Sumner was a Conscience Whig. For 10 points, name this crop, whose seeds were removed by Eli Whitney’s gin.

tossups.p: Edgar Degas [“day-GAH”] painted his uncle’s New Orleans business in 1873, showing men in top hats reading a newspaper and examining samples of this white fiber spread on a table. New Orleans was a leading port for shipping this crop to mills in Europe.
tossups.r: Eli Whitney’s gin removed its seeds. For 10 points, name this crop, the South’s most valuable export before the Civil War.

tossups.p: Mohandas Gandhi urged Indians to spin their own thread on a spinning wheel called a charkha [“CHAR-kuh”] and to wear homespun khadi [“KAH-dee”] cloth instead of cloth woven from this fiber in British mills. Much of the raw material for those British mills had come from the American South.
tossups.r: Its fluffy fibers grow in a boll around the seeds. For 10 points, name this crop cleaned by Eli Whitney’s 1793 gin.

tossups.p: Soviet planners diverted the rivers that fed the Aral Sea to irrigate huge fields of this thirsty crop in Central Asia, and the sea shrank to a fraction of its former size. The Indus Valley civilization was one of the first to spin and weave this plant’s fibers into cloth.
tossups.r: In the United States, it was the leading crop of the Deep South. For 10 points, name this fiber cleaned by Eli Whitney’s gin.

tossups.p: Solomon Northup described how enslaved workers on Edwin Epps’s Louisiana plantation had to pick this crop from dawn to dark and were punished if their baskets weighed too little. Northup told that story in his 1853 memoir _Twelve Years a Slave_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this crop whose spread after the invention of Eli Whitney’s gin made slavery grow across the Deep South.

tossups.p: James Hargreaves’s spinning jenny and Richard Arkwright’s water frame were used to spin thread from this fiber, helping to start the Industrial Revolution in Britain. Manchester, England, became the world’s leading center for turning it into cloth.
tossups.r: Much of Manchester’s raw supply came from the American South. For 10 points, name this crop cleaned by Eli Whitney’s gin.

tossups.p: In 1861, many Southerners refused to ship this crop to Europe, hoping that shortages would pressure Britain and France into recognizing the Confederacy. That plan failed, partly because British warehouses already held large supplies from earlier bumper harvests.
tossups.r: Southerners had boasted that this crop was “King.” For 10 points, name this crop that dominated the economy of the antebellum South.

tossups.p: George Washington Carver taught Southern farmers to rotate this soil-exhausting crop with peanuts and sweet potatoes. After the Civil War, many sharecroppers grew this crop and fell deep into debt under the crop-lien system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this crop picked by hand across the Deep South, whose seeds were removed by Eli Whitney’s gin.

tossups.p: By 1860, this crop made up more than half of all U.S. exports by value. Its fields had spread west from South Carolina and Georgia across Alabama and Mississippi all the way to Texas, with some of the richest land in the Mississippi Delta.
tossups.r: Nearly four million people were enslaved in the South by then. For 10 points, name this cash crop, whose seeds were removed by Eli Whitney’s gin.

tossups.p: Long-staple varieties of this plant grew well on the Sea Islands off Georgia and South Carolina, but short-staple upland varieties had sticky green seeds that were very hard to remove by hand. This shrub belongs to the mallow family, and its fibers are about 90 percent cellulose.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this crop, whose fibers grow inside a boll and were cleaned by Eli Whitney’s gin.

clues.t: Eli Whitney’s gin (1793) quickly pulled the seeds out of its fibers
Its spread across the Deep South made slavery grow; nearly 4 million people were enslaved by 1860
The South’s main cash crop; its fluffy white fibers grow in a boll around the seeds
Southerners boasted that it was “King” of the antebellum economy
Spun and woven into cloth in textile mills in New England and Britain
The boll weevil, a beetle from Mexico, reached Texas in the 1890s and ruined crops across the South
Lowell, Massachusetts: young “mill girls” worked in its textile mills and published the _Lowell Offering_
Samuel Slater, “Father of the American Industrial Revolution,” built a spinning mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island
The Confederacy held it back in 1861 to win British support, but Britain had stockpiles and found new sources in Egypt and India
George Washington Carver taught farmers to rotate it with peanuts and sweet potatoes to restore the soil
After the Civil War, many sharecroppers grew it and fell into debt under the crop-lien system
The gin made short-staple “upland” types profitable; long-staple types grew on the Sea Islands
Senator James Henry Hammond (1858): “You dare not make war” on it, because it “is king”
Lancashire “famine” (1861–1865): British mills ran short during the Civil War; Lincoln thanked the workingmen of Manchester (1863)
Enterprise, Alabama, built a monument to the boll weevil (1919) for pushing farmers to grow peanuts
A shrub in the mallow family; its fibers are about 90 percent cellulose
Whitney built the gin at Mulberry Grove, the Georgia plantation of Catharine Greene, widow of General Nathanael Greene
The gin’s wire teeth pulled fibers through slots too narrow for the seeds; Whitney earned little because planters copied it
By 1860 it made up more than half of all U.S. exports by value
In the 1840s, Massachusetts Whigs tied to the mills, nicknamed for this crop, split from the antislavery “Conscience Whigs” like Charles Sumner
Edgar Degas painted his uncle’s New Orleans office, where buyers examined samples of it (1873)
Mohandas Gandhi spun thread on a charkha and wore homespun khadi to protest cloth made in British mills
Soviet irrigation of Central Asian fields of it drained much of the Aral Sea
Solomon Northup described picking it on Edwin Epps’s Louisiana plantation in _Twelve Years a Slave_ (1853)
Britain’s spinning jenny (Hargreaves) and water frame (Arkwright) spun it into thread; Manchester became the world’s leading center for making it into cloth
The Indus Valley civilization was one of the first to spin and weave it into cloth

trap.title: Crop, machine, or inventor?
trap.body: Tossups on cotton, on Eli Whitney, and on the cotton gin share the same clues: Mulberry Grove, wire teeth, sticky seeds, and the spread of slavery. If the question asks for “this crop” or “this plant,” answering “cotton gin” is wrong. Other Southern cash crops can trick you too: tobacco saved Jamestown, Eliza Lucas Pinckney grew indigo in South Carolina, and rice and sugar grew in the Carolinas and Louisiana.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this crop,” “this fiber,” or “this plant” wants cotton; “this machine” or “this device” wants the cotton gin; “this inventor” wants Eli Whitney. Boll weevils, “King,” the Lowell mills, and Lancashire all point to cotton.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cotton (accept Gossypium; prompt on “cash crop”; do not accept “cotton gin”)

topics.name: Erie Canal
topics.kicker: Waterway from the Hudson River to Lake Erie · Opened the West to trade
topics.briefing: Critics laughed at Governor DeWitt Clinton’s plan to dig a 363-mile ditch across New York from the Hudson River to Lake Erie, calling it “Clinton’s Ditch.” Workers dug it largely by hand, and when the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it cut the cost of shipping goods by about 90 percent. Farm goods from the Midwest poured east, and New York City became the busiest port in the country.
topics.answerHtml: Erie Canal (accept “Clinton’s Ditch”; prompt on “Erie” or “canal” alone; do not accept “Lake Erie”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Digging on this project began at Rome, New York, on July 4, 1817, and its middle section, between Rome and Utica, was the first part to open. When the whole project was finished eight years later, its 83 locks could raise boats more than 500 feet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal championed by Governor DeWitt Clinton, which linked the Hudson River to the Great Lakes.

tossups.p: Thomas Jefferson reportedly called the idea for this project “little short of madness,” and James Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill, which could have helped pay for projects like it. Without federal money, New York State spent about seven million dollars to build it.
tossups.r: Governor DeWitt Clinton championed it. For 10 points, name this canal that opened in 1825, linking Albany and Buffalo.

tossups.p: When this project opened, cannons placed along its route fired one after another to relay the news to New York City. A governor then rode the boat _Seneca Chief_ across the state and poured a keg of lake water into the Atlantic Ocean.
tossups.r: That ceremony, led by DeWitt Clinton, was called the “Wedding of the Waters.” For 10 points, name this New York canal.

tossups.p: At Lockport, two side-by-side sets of five locks called the “Flight of Five” lifted boats up the Niagara Escarpment along this waterway. Farther east, stone aqueducts carried it over rivers, including the Genesee [“jen-uh-SEE”] River at Rochester.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal that connected the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo.

tossups.p: A 1905 song by Thomas S. Allen describes a mule named Sal towing a boat on this waterway and warns, “Low bridge, everybody down.” Mules and horses walking along its towpath pulled the boats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York canal, which opened in 1825 and was championed by DeWitt Clinton.

tossups.p: This waterway cut the cost of shipping goods across New York by about 90 percent, and its tolls soon paid back the cost of building it. It helped New York City become the busiest port in the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal built by New York State between 1817 and 1825.

tossups.p: This waterway followed the valley of the Mohawk River, a low gap through the Appalachian Mountains that gave it an advantage over routes farther south. Its success set off a wave of canal building in Ohio, Pennsylvania, and other states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal that linked the Great Lakes to New York City by way of the Hudson River.

tossups.p: This project’s greatest supporter, a former mayor of New York City, had lost the 1812 presidential election to James Madison before becoming governor of New York. Critics mocked the project as “the Big Ditch” and named it after him.
tossups.r: That governor was DeWitt Clinton. For 10 points, name this canal, which opened in 1825.

tossups.p: Canvass White found a way to make cement from local limestone that hardened underwater, and it was used to build this waterway’s locks. Many of the men who dug it were local farmers and Irish immigrants working with shovels, picks, and horses.
tossups.r: It opened in 1825. For 10 points, name this canal across New York, championed by DeWitt Clinton.

tossups.p: Religious revivals swept the towns along this waterway so often that the region was called the “burned-over district.” In 1830, Joseph Smith published the _Book of Mormon_ in Palmyra, a town on its route.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal, opened in 1825, that made Rochester and Buffalo into boomtowns.

tossups.p: This waterway was widened in the mid-1800s and later replaced by the larger New York State Barge Canal, which was completed in 1918. Its original channel was 40 feet wide and only 4 feet deep.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 363-mile canal between Albany and Buffalo, which opened in 1825.

tossups.p: This waterway let farmers in Ohio, Indiana, and Michigan ship wheat and flour east cheaply, and it carried thousands of settlers west. Rochester shipped so much flour on it that the city was nicknamed the “Flour City.”
tossups.r: Governor DeWitt Clinton had pushed for it. For 10 points, name this New York canal that opened in 1825.

tossups.p: Because few Americans had formal engineering training, chief engineer Benjamin Wright and his assistants learned on the job while building this project, which became known as America’s first school of engineering. Wright is often called the “Father of American Civil Engineering.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal that opened in 1825, linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie.

tossups.p: Boats on this waterway were weighed at special locks to set their tolls, and the last surviving weighlock building, in Syracuse, later became a museum about it. Barrels of salt from Syracuse were among the many goods it carried.
tossups.r: DeWitt Clinton championed it. For 10 points, name this canal that linked Albany and Buffalo, opening in 1825.

tossups.p: Gouverneur Morris led a state commission that began planning this waterway in 1810, years before New York’s legislature approved building it in 1817. Its builders had to dig through the Montezuma Marsh, where many workers fell ill with malaria.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal, championed by DeWitt Clinton, that linked the Hudson River to the Great Lakes.

clues.t: Linked the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo, across upstate New York
Championed by Governor DeWitt Clinton; critics called it his “Ditch” or his “Folly”
Opened in 1825 after about eight years of digging (begun 1817)
Gave the Great Lakes and the Midwest a water route to New York City and the Atlantic Ocean
Helped make New York City the nation’s busiest port and New York the “Empire State”
“Wedding of the Waters” (1825): Clinton poured a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic after riding the _Seneca Chief_
Originally 363 miles long, 40 feet wide, and 4 feet deep, with 83 locks
Mules and horses on a towpath pulled the boats; the song “Low Bridge, Everybody Down” is about a mule named Sal
Cut shipping costs by about 90 percent; New York State paid about $7 million to build it
Boomtowns along it included Rochester (the “Flour City”), Syracuse, Utica, Lockport, and Buffalo
Followed the Mohawk River valley, a low gap through the Appalachian Mountains
Its success set off a canal-building boom in Ohio, Pennsylvania, and other states
Digging began at Rome, New York, on July 4, 1817; the first section opened between Rome and Utica
Lockport’s “Flight of Five” locks lifted boats up the Niagara Escarpment
Thomas Jefferson reportedly called the idea “little short of madness”
James Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill (1817), so New York built it without federal money
Chief engineer Benjamin Wright (“Father of American Civil Engineering”); Canvass White made a cement that hardens underwater
Widened in the 1800s and replaced by the New York State Barge Canal (1918)
Local farmers and Irish immigrants did much of the digging; many workers fell ill with malaria in the Montezuma Marsh
Ran through the “burned-over district” of religious revivals; Joseph Smith published the _Book of Mormon_ in Palmyra (1830)
Stone aqueducts carried it over rivers, such as the Genesee River at Rochester
DeWitt Clinton, a former New York City mayor, had lost the 1812 presidential election to James Madison
Gouverneur Morris led the state commission that began planning it in 1810
When it opened, cannons fired one after another along its route to relay the news to New York City
Boats were weighed at weighlocks to set tolls; Syracuse’s weighlock building became a museum

trap.title: Canal, lake, or railroad?
trap.body: The word “Erie” leads to three different answers. The Erie Canal is the 1825 waterway across New York, Lake Erie is where Oliver Hazard Perry won his 1813 battle, and the Erie Railroad was fought over in the 1868 Erie War. Erie Canal clues like “Clinton’s Ditch” and the “Wedding of the Waters” also show up in tossups whose answer is New York State or Governor DeWitt Clinton.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this canal” or “this waterway” wants the Erie Canal, “this governor” wants DeWitt Clinton, and “this state” wants New York. Say the whole name, “Erie Canal,” because “Erie” alone may only earn a prompt. “Clinton’s Ditch” is also accepted.
trap.line: Real answer line: Erie Canal (accept “Clinton’s Ditch”; prompt on “Erie” or “canal” alone; do not accept “Lake Erie”)

topics.name: Filibuster
topics.kicker: Senate tactic of endless debate · Stopped by a cloture vote
topics.briefing: In the U.S. Senate, debate on a bill usually has no time limit unless enough senators vote to stop it. A filibuster uses that freedom to delay or block a vote, sometimes with marathon speeches: in 1957, Strom Thurmond talked for 24 hours and 18 minutes. Since 1975, ending debate on most bills has taken three-fifths of the Senate, usually 60 votes, through a process called cloture.
topics.answerHtml: Filibuster (accept word forms like filibustering or filibusterer; prompt on unlimited debate; do not accept “cloture”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Aaron Burr suggested that the Senate drop its rarely used “previous question” motion. After the Senate removed that motion in 1806, it had no rule letting a majority cut off debate, which eventually made this tactic possible.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Senate tactic of using long debate to block a bill, which can be ended by a cloture vote.

tossups.p: In 1917, Woodrow Wilson denounced “a little group of willful men, representing no opinion but their own,” after Robert La Follette and other senators used this tactic to stop a bill arming merchant ships.
tossups.r: The Senate then adopted Rule XXII, its first rule for ending debate by a cloture vote. For 10 points, name this delaying tactic.

tossups.p: During a speech of more than fifteen hours in 1935, Senator Huey Long of Louisiana read from Shakespeare and explained how to fry oysters and make potlikker [“POT-lik-er”]. Long, a critic of Franklin Roosevelt, often used this tactic in the 1930s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Senate tactic of delaying a vote by talking, which can be ended by cloture.

tossups.p: Years before he switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party, a senator from South Carolina used this tactic for 24 hours and 18 minutes, trying to block the Civil Rights Act of 1957. It was the longest speech in Senate history until 2025.
tossups.r: That senator was Strom Thurmond. For 10 points, name this Senate tactic that can be ended by a cloture vote.

tossups.p: Robert Byrd of West Virginia spoke for more than 14 hours in June 1964, near the end of a months-long use of this tactic against the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Southern senators had taken turns speaking since March.
tossups.r: Soon afterward, the Senate voted to end debate on a civil rights bill for the first time, a vote called cloture. For 10 points, name this Senate delaying tactic.

tossups.p: In a 1939 Frank Capra film, Jimmy Stewart plays a new senator who uses this tactic, talking for nearly a full day to clear his name and stop a corrupt dam project, until he collapses on the Senate floor.
tossups.r: That film is _Mr. Smith Goes to Washington_. For 10 points, name this tactic of talking nonstop to delay a Senate vote.

tossups.p: In 2013, Senate Democrats changed the chamber’s rules so that most presidential nominations could no longer be blocked by this tactic, a move nicknamed the “nuclear option.” In 2017, Senate Republicans did the same for Supreme Court nominations during the confirmation of Neil Gorsuch.
tossups.r: Ending it requires a cloture vote. For 10 points, name this delaying tactic that, for most bills, takes 60 votes to end.

tossups.p: In the 1850s, this word described American adventurers like William Walker, who led a private army into Nicaragua and made himself its president in 1856. The word comes from a Spanish term for a pirate or freebooter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, give this word that, in the U.S. Senate, means a long speech or debate used to delay a vote.

tossups.p: Narciso López [“LOH-pez”] launched armed expeditions from the United States to try to take Cuba from Spain in 1850 and 1851, and he was executed in Havana. Men like López and William Walker were known by this term.
tossups.r: For 10 points, give this term that also names a long Senate speech meant to delay a vote.

tossups.p: The first successful vote to end this tactic came in 1919, cutting off debate on the Treaty of Versailles. Two years earlier, a new Senate rule had allowed two-thirds of the senators voting to end it.
tossups.r: That rule created cloture. For 10 points, name this Senate tactic of delaying a vote through long debate.

tossups.p: In 1922, Southern senators used this tactic to stop the Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill, even though it had passed the House of Representatives. For decades afterward, Southern senators used it to block civil rights bills.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tactic of refusing to end debate in the U.S. Senate, which can be stopped by cloture.

tossups.p: Budget reconciliation bills cannot be blocked by this tactic, because Senate debate on them is limited to 20 hours. Since the 1970s, a “two-track” system has let the Senate move on to other business while this tactic is under way, so senators rarely have to keep talking.
tossups.r: It can be ended by a vote called cloture. For 10 points, name this Senate delaying tactic.

tossups.p: In 1975, the Senate changed the number of votes needed to end this tactic from two-thirds of the senators voting to three-fifths of all senators. Ending it on a proposal to change the Senate’s own rules still takes a two-thirds vote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Senate tactic of using endless debate to block a vote, which can be ended by cloture.

tossups.p: In 2013, Rand Paul of Kentucky held the Senate floor for nearly 13 hours to delay a vote on John Brennan’s nomination as CIA director, raising questions about drone strikes. Unlike most modern uses of this tactic, his was a “talking” one, in which he had to stay on the floor.
tossups.r: It can be ended by cloture. For 10 points, name this Senate tactic of talking to block or delay a vote.

tossups.p: To end this tactic, at least 16 senators must sign a motion, and the Senate votes on it two days after it is filed. Even after that vote succeeds, senators may still debate most bills for up to 30 more hours.
tossups.r: That process is called cloture, and it usually needs 60 votes. For 10 points, name this Senate delaying tactic.

trap.title: The tactic or its cure?
trap.body: Many clues about this tactic are really about the vote that ends it. Cloture is the motion to cut off debate, created by Rule XXII in 1917 and usually needing 60 votes, so answering one when the question wants the other is wrong. The word also has an older meaning: 1800s adventurers like William Walker and Narciso López were called filibusters too.
trap.fix: Ask whether the clue is about keeping debate going or stopping it. Talking for hours, Strom Thurmond, Huey Long’s recipes, and _Mr. Smith Goes to Washington_ mean the filibuster; Rule XXII, three-fifths, and “invoking” a vote mean cloture. Don’t confuse it with a veto, which only the president can use.
trap.line: Real answer line: Filibuster (accept word forms like filibustering or filibusterer; prompt on unlimited debate; do not accept “cloture”)

topics.name: Fort Ticonderoga
topics.kicker: Fort on Lake Champlain · Captured by Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys
topics.briefing: Built by the French in the 1750s where Lake George drains into Lake Champlain, Fort Ticonderoga guarded the water highway between Canada and the Hudson River. In 1758, a small French army defended it against a British force several times larger. In May 1775, Ethan Allen, Benedict Arnold, and the Green Mountain Boys seized it in a surprise dawn raid, and that winter Henry Knox hauled its cannons all the way to Boston.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The French engineer Michel Chartier de Lotbinière [“lot-been-YAIR”] designed this star-shaped fort in the 1750s on a point of land where the outlet of Lake George flows into a much longer lake. The French called it Carillon [“kah-ree-YOHN”].
tossups.r: In 1775, the Green Mountain Boys captured it. For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain, whose cannons Henry Knox later hauled to Boston.

tossups.p: Lord George Howe was killed in a skirmish two days before a British army under James Abercromby attacked this fort in July 1758. The much smaller French force of the Marquis de Montcalm [“mont-KAHM”] won by defending log walls protected by an abatis [“AB-uh-tee”] of sharpened, felled trees.
tossups.r: The French called it Carillon. For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain, which Ethan Allen captured in 1775.

tossups.p: Scottish Highlanders of the Black Watch suffered hundreds of casualties charging this fort’s defenses in 1758, during the French and Indian War. The British finally took it the next year, when Jeffery Amherst’s army arrived and the retreating French blew up part of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort near the southern end of Lake Champlain, captured by Ethan Allen in 1775.

tossups.p: This fort was captured at dawn on May 10, 1775, the same day the Second Continental Congress first met in Philadelphia. Its British commander, Captain William Delaplace, surrendered his small garrison after the attackers rushed in by surprise.
tossups.r: Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold led that attack. For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain.

tossups.p: According to his own later account, a frontiersman demanded that this fort surrender “in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress.” He shared command of the attack with an officer who carried a commission from Massachusetts and later became a traitor.
tossups.r: Those men were Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold. For 10 points, name this fort captured in 1775.

tossups.p: In the winter of 1775 to 1776, a former Boston bookseller used sleds pulled by oxen to haul about 60 tons of cannons from this fort across frozen rivers and the Berkshire Mountains. He called his convoy a “noble train of artillery.”
tossups.r: That man was Henry Knox. For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain that the Green Mountain Boys had captured.

tossups.p: Cannons taken from this fort were secretly placed on Dorchester Heights in March 1776, forcing General William Howe’s British army to leave Boston on March 17. Boston’s county still celebrates that day as Evacuation Day.
tossups.r: Henry Knox had hauled those cannons from this fort. For 10 points, name this fort that Ethan Allen captured in 1775.

tossups.p: In July 1777, John Burgoyne’s army hauled cannons to the top of Mount Defiance, a hill overlooking this fort, so General Arthur St. Clair abandoned the fort. Congress then removed Philip Schuyler [“SKY-ler”] from command, and St. Clair faced a court-martial but was found not guilty.
tossups.r: Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga that October. For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain, which Ethan Allen had captured two years earlier.

tossups.p: The Pell family bought the ruins of this fort and restored it, opening it to visitors as a museum in 1909. Its name comes from a Mohawk word meaning roughly “at the junction of two waterways.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort near the southern end of Lake Champlain, which Ethan Allen captured in 1775.

tossups.p: U.S. Navy ships, including a World War II aircraft carrier and a class of guided-missile cruisers, share this fort’s name. The fort guarded the narrow passage between Lake George and a much longer lake to the north.
tossups.r: A well-known brand of yellow pencils shares its name too. For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain, which Ethan Allen captured in 1775.

tossups.p: Within days after this fort fell, Seth Warner led men who captured nearby Crown Point, and Benedict Arnold sailed north to raid Fort St. Johns in Canada. Those moves briefly gave the Americans control of the lake route to Canada.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort that Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys took on May 10, 1775.

tossups.p: In 1757, the Marquis de Montcalm [“mont-KAHM”] gathered his army at this French fort before moving south along Lake George to capture Fort William Henry, an event described in _The Last of the Mohicans_. Robert Rogers’s rangers often scouted the woods around this fort.
tossups.r: The British renamed it after capturing it in 1759. For 10 points, name this fort later captured by Ethan Allen in 1775.

tossups.p: This fort guarded the water route that ran from the St. Lawrence River up the Richelieu [“RISH-uh-loo”] River and across a long lake toward the Hudson River, the main invasion path between Canada and New York. British general John Burgoyne retook it in 1777.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain, captured by Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold in 1775.

tossups.p: After defeating Benedict Arnold’s small fleet near Valcour Island in October 1776, the British general Guy Carleton decided it was too late in the year to attack this fort and pulled back to Canada. The fort fell to the British the next summer instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain whose cannons Henry Knox had hauled to Boston.

tossups.p: The French began building this fort in late 1755, soon after William Johnson’s army of colonists and Mohawk allies defeated Baron Dieskau [“DEES-kow”] at the Battle of Lake George. It was meant to block any British advance from the south toward Canada.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort on Lake Champlain, captured by the Green Mountain Boys in 1775.

trap.title: Which lake fort?
trap.body: Several forts and battle sites along Lake Champlain and Lake George turn up in the same tossups. Fort William Henry was Montcalm’s 1757 target in _The Last of the Mohicans_, Crown Point was taken by Seth Warner days after Ticonderoga fell, and Saratoga is where Burgoyne surrendered after capturing Ticonderoga in 1777. Early clues from the French and Indian War may also call this fort Carillon.
trap.fix: Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys, Henry Knox’s cannons, Montcalm’s 1758 win over Abercromby, and Mount Defiance all mean Fort Ticonderoga. If you know only the French name, say “Fort Carillon,” which is accepted. Fort Necessity (Washington, 1754) and Fort Duquesne (Pittsburgh) are different forts, far to the south and west.
trap.line: Real answer line: Fort Ticonderoga (accept Fort Carillon; prompt on Carillon alone)

topics.name: Frederick Douglass
topics.kicker: Abolitionist who escaped slavery · Author, editor, and great orator
topics.briefing: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland and kept teaching himself to read after his lessons were forbidden. In 1838 he escaped by train and steamboat, disguised as a sailor, and soon became one of the most powerful speakers in America. His 1845 autobiography became a bestseller, and his Rochester newspaper, _The North Star_, demanded freedom for enslaved people and equal rights for women.
topics.answerHtml: Frederick Douglass (accept Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey; do not accept “Stephen Douglas”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a boy in Baltimore, this man bought a copy of _The Columbian Orator_, a book of famous speeches, and traded bread to white boys in the street in exchange for reading lessons. Earlier, Sophia Auld had taught him the alphabet until her husband made her stop.
tossups.r: He later wrote about these lessons in his 1845 _Narrative_. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who founded the newspaper _The North Star_.

tossups.p: In one autobiography, this man described fighting back against Edward Covey, a farmer known as a “slave breaker,” and wrote, “You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.” Covey never tried to whip him again.
tossups.r: He later founded the newspaper _The North Star_. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who described that fight in his 1845 _Narrative_.

tossups.p: In September 1838, this man escaped from Baltimore dressed as a sailor and carrying papers borrowed from a free Black seaman, traveling by train and steamboat to New York. Anna Murray, a free Black woman who had helped him plan the escape, soon joined him there, and they married.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who became a famous abolitionist speaker and wrote an 1845 _Narrative_ of his life.

tossups.p: After escaping slavery, this man settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where his host, Nathan Johnson, suggested a new last name taken from a character in Walter Scott’s poem _The Lady of the Lake_. He had been born with the last name Bailey.
tossups.r: He later wrote three autobiographies. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who published the antislavery newspaper _The North Star_.

tossups.p: After this man spoke at an antislavery meeting on Nantucket in 1841, the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society hired him as a lecturer. He later broke with that society’s leader, William Lloyd Garrison, by arguing that the Constitution could be used to fight slavery.
tossups.r: Garrison had called the Constitution a proslavery document. For 10 points, name this former slave who founded _The North Star_ in Rochester, New York.

tossups.p: Speaking to the Rochester Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society on July 5, 1852, this man said that, to an enslaved person, the nation’s holiday celebration was “a sham.” He told the crowd, “You may rejoice, I must mourn.”
tossups.r: That speech asked, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” For 10 points, name this abolitionist who had escaped slavery in Maryland.

tossups.p: This man’s newspaper used the motto “Right is of no sex, Truth is of no color.” In 1848, he spoke up for a resolution demanding women’s right to vote at the Seneca Falls Convention.
tossups.r: That newspaper, _The North Star_, was printed in Rochester, New York. For 10 points, name this abolitionist and former slave.

tossups.p: Fearing recapture after his first autobiography made him famous, this man spent nearly two years lecturing in Britain and Ireland, where he met Daniel O’Connell. In 1846, British supporters raised money to buy his freedom legally.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist who wrote an 1845 _Narrative_ of his life and founded _The North Star_.

tossups.p: In 1859, John Brown met this man at a stone quarry near Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, and asked him to join a raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry. This man refused, but after the raid he fled to Canada and then England to avoid arrest.
tossups.r: He had escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who published _The North Star_.

tossups.p: Two of this man’s sons, Lewis and Charles, joined the 54th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment after he helped recruit Black soldiers for it. In 1863, he met Abraham Lincoln at the White House to push for equal pay and fair treatment for Black troops.
tossups.r: His 1845 _Narrative_ had made him famous. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who had escaped slavery in 1838.

tossups.p: From 1889 to 1891, this man served as the U.S. minister to Haiti, and at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago he represented Haiti at its pavilion. With Ida B. Wells, he wrote a pamphlet protesting that Black Americans had been left out of that fair.
tossups.r: Decades earlier, he had escaped slavery in Maryland. For 10 points, name this famous abolitionist, who wrote an 1845 _Narrative_ of his life.

tossups.p: This man’s only work of fiction, _The Heroic Slave_, tells the story of Madison Washington, who led a revolt of enslaved people aboard the ship _Creole_ in 1841. This man also wrote three autobiographies, including _My Bondage and My Freedom_.
tossups.r: He had escaped slavery by disguising himself as a sailor. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who published the newspaper _The North Star_.

tossups.p: Rutherford B. Hayes appointed this man U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia in 1877. This man spent his last years at Cedar Hill, his home in Washington’s Anacostia neighborhood, where he died in 1895, hours after attending a women’s rights meeting.
tossups.r: He had founded _The North Star_ decades earlier. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who had escaped slavery in Maryland.

tossups.p: In 1872, without asking him, the Equal Rights Party nominated this man for vice president on a ticket with Victoria Woodhull. Years earlier, he had declared, “If there is no struggle, there is no progress.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist and newspaper editor who wrote an 1845 _Narrative_ of his life.

tossups.p: In 1876, this man gave the main speech when the Emancipation Memorial, a statue of Abraham Lincoln paid for by formerly enslaved people, was unveiled in Washington, D.C. Two years earlier, he had briefly led the Freedman’s Savings Bank just before it collapsed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist whose famous speeches included “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”

trap.title: Douglass, not Douglas
trap.body: Two famous figures of the 1850s share almost the same name. Frederick Douglass (two s’s) was the abolitionist editor, while Stephen A. Douglas (one s) was the Illinois senator who debated Abraham Lincoln and wrote the Kansas-Nebraska Act. Players also buzz too early with other abolitionists: William Lloyd Garrison published _The Liberator_, and Harriet Tubman led people north on the Underground Railroad.
trap.fix: _The North Star_, the 1845 _Narrative_, the sailor disguise, Edward Covey, and “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” mean Frederick Douglass. The Lincoln-Douglas debates, popular sovereignty, and the “Little Giant” mean Stephen Douglas. Say “Frederick Douglass” in full if you have any doubt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Frederick Douglass (accept Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey; do not accept “Stephen Douglas”)
